script.title: Waititu 13-Year Graft Sentence, Sh6,000 PIN Bribes, and More
script.summary: Former Kiambu governor Ferdinand Waititu faces 13 years in prison over an irregular Sh588.7 million road tender as a new study exposes Sh6,000 bribes for free KRA PINs. Here is your weekly breakdown of the official record covering press freedom, shrinking family sizes, and tax enforcement in Kenya.
script.intro: A service that the law says is completely free is costing ordinary Kenyans up to Sh6,000 in bribes. This week, we look at that fresh finding from the World Bank. We also examine a 13-year prison sentence handed to a former governor over a county road tender. Along with that, we cover shrinking family sizes, documented attacks on journalists, and two major tax notices. Here is what the official record shows across Kenya.

stories.script: On 2 November, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights documented 92 attacks against journalists across the country. Their record covers press freedom violations committed over the past year. Security officers caused most of the physical injuries while journalists were covering public protests and rallies. The commission stresses that journalists must work safely so that Kenyans can receive verified facts to hold leaders accountable. When journalists face beatings and intimidation, wananchi lose verified reporting on how taxes and basic rights are handled. Silencing the press hides the truth from ordinary citizens who need reliable information every day. A free press protects the right of every Kenyan to know what is happening in the country. Following these findings, Kenyans demand that the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions prosecutes every officer involved in these assaults. The human rights body is asking the public to report any attack on reporters through their toll-free line, 0800 720 627. The next step rests with the authorities to see if those officers face prosecution.

stories.chapter: Kenyan Fertility Falls to Three Children
stories.script: New demographic data released this week by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics shows that families are shrinking across Kenya. According to the bureau, Kenyan women now have an average of 3 children, down from 4 children in 2022. The survey also reveals that teenage pregnancy dropped to 11.9 percent this year across the country. The statistics bureau confirms that this 11.9 percent mark is the lowest teenage pregnancy rate on official record. For ordinary citizens, having 3 children instead of 4 means fewer dependents per household than four years ago. At the same time, fewer teenage pregnancies mean that more schoolgirls can stay in school and finish their education. Together, these numbers show that household sizes are steadily dropping compared to what was recorded in 2022. Kenyans can inspect the complete survey on the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics portal at knbs.or.ke. The coming years will show how this drop in dependents shapes daily household budgets nationwide.

On 2 November, the Anti-Corruption Court handed former Kiambu governor Ferdinand Waititu a 13-year jail sentence over graft. The court ruled that Waititu must either serve 13 years in prison or pay a fine of Sh21 million. This conviction followed a case prosecuted by the DPP regarding an irregular Sh588.7 million Kiambu county road tender. The court found that public funds were lost through this fraudulent county road procurement process. For ordinary taxpayers, money lost in fraudulent county tenders directly delays the construction of vital roads and health centres. Taxpayers carry the burden when roads remain unfinished and local health clinics fail to open as planned. Following the ruling, Kenyans demand that the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission recovers all stolen assets from county tenders. Citizens who want to study the full conviction can check the ruling on the judiciary website at judiciary.go.ke. All eyes now turn to the anti-graft commission to see how much stolen county money will actually be returned.

stories.chapter: World Bank Finds Sh6,000 PIN Bribes
stories.script: On 5 November, a new World Bank study revealed that Kenyans are paying an average of Sh6,000 in bribes. These illegal payments are being made just to obtain a Kenya Revenue Authority personal identification number. By law, getting a KRA PIN is completely free of charge for every citizen. Yet the World Bank report shows that corrupt officers extort money from citizens seeking this basic registration. This unfair financial burden falls heavily on young job seekers and youth trying to register small business permits. When citizens must part with scarce cash for free services, entering the formal economy becomes even harder. Kenyans are calling on the Kenya Revenue Authority to stop its officers from selling services that should cost nothing. Anyone who encounters an officer asking for a bribe can report them to the EACC toll-free hotline on 1176. Cleaning up that registration counter will show whether KRA is serious about protecting ordinary job seekers.

stories.chapter: Sh47 Billion Lost to Fake Cigarettes
stories.script: While some citizens pay bribes for tax numbers, the government is losing billions from untaxed tobacco sales. A new 2026 study finds that illicit cigarettes cost Kenya Sh47 billion every year in lost tax revenue. This illegal business runs on smuggled and counterfeit cigarette packs that skip official Kenya Revenue Authority excise stamps. Every packet sold without a legitimate stamp robs the public purse of money meant for vital public projects. That lost Sh47 billion could have funded government programs, local schools, public hospitals, and road networks across the country. Instead, criminal cartels pocket the profits while public infrastructure suffers from lack of funding. Citizens are advised to check for official KRA excise stamps before buying cigarettes and report vendors selling unstamped packs. Kenyans want the tax agency to tighten its stamp inspections across distribution channels and retail outlets nationwide. The challenge now is whether enforcement teams can shut down the smuggling networks that drain this tax revenue.

The Kenya Revenue Authority issued a strict compliance directive to employers across the country on 6 November. The tax authority reminded all employers that they must remit statutory employee levies by the 9th day of every month. These mandatory deductions affect millions of Kenyan workers who earn a living in the formal sector. When an employer fails to send deducted money to the tax authority, workers risk losing their hard-earned statutory benefits. Unremitted deductions also leave employees facing unnecessary administrative headaches with the taxman down the road. Workers are encouraged to check their payslips regularly to confirm that all deducted taxes actually reach the tax authority. Kenyan employees are insisting that business owners submit these deductions on time each month without fail. Pay attention to your next salary slip to verify that your deductions reflect correctly on your official tax ledger.
